issue.issue_text: Whether the plea of misjoinder of charges can be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court when it was not raised in the High Court or in the petition for special leave.

facts: The appellants raised the plea of misjoinder of charges for the first time before the Supreme Court.
This point was not argued in the High Court, as there was no mention of it in that court's judgment.
The issue of misjoinder of charges was also not included in the petition for special leave to appeal.
law: A party cannot be permitted to raise a new issue at the Supreme Court stage if it was not raised in the lower courts or in the petition for special leave.
An error, omission, or misjoinder of charges is not considered a valid ground to invalidate a conviction unless the court concludes that it has caused a "failure of justice."
In determining whether a failure of justice has occurred, the court must consider whether an objection could have been raised at an earlier stage in the proceedings.
application: The Court noted that the appellants had failed to raise the issue of misjoinder of charges at two prior opportunities: before the High Court and in their special leave petition.
Because the issue was not raised at these earlier stages, the Court applied its procedural rule and barred the appellants from arguing the point for the first time during the final hearing.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the plea of misjoinder of charges, holding that the appellants could not be permitted to raise this question for the first time at such a late stage of the proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether a conviction for a substantive offence can be set aside due to the absence of, or an error in, the charge, without the accused demonstrating that prejudice was caused and a failure of justice occurred.

facts: The accused was convicted under Section 302/34 of the Indian Penal Code (murder with common intention).
There was an omission to formally frame the charge under Section 302, although the gist of the charge sheet clearly indicated the accusation.
The accused did not argue before the trial court or the High Court that the absence of the charge caused them prejudice or led to a failure of justice.
A similarly situated co-accused had their appeal dismissed by the Supreme Court.
law: Section 464 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, states that a finding, sentence, or order of a court is not invalid merely due to the absence of, or an error in, a charge.
An exception to this rule exists only if the court of appeal finds that a "failure of justice has in fact been occasioned thereby."
The burden is on the accused to show that the defect in the charge caused them prejudice, leading to a failure of justice.

A failure of justice occurs if the accused was unaware of the actual charge, could not mount a proper defense, and was therefore denied a fair trial. Conversely, if the accused's defense shows they understood and defended against the real charge, no prejudice is inferred.
application: The Court applied Section 464 of the Cr.P.C., noting that the absence of a formal charge does not automatically invalidate the conviction.
It found that the accused had failed to meet their burden of proof, as they never demonstrated, or even argued, that any prejudice was caused or that a failure of justice occurred.

The Court observed that the charge sheet's content made the accusation of murder clear, implying the accused was aware of what they were being tried for and had a fair opportunity to defend themselves.
Therefore, the Court concluded that the omission in the charge did not occasion a failure of justice in this case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that a conviction for a substantive offence cannot be set aside due to an absent or erroneous charge unless the accused specifically demonstrates that the defect caused them prejudice and resulted in a failure of justice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the plea of misjoinder of charges can be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court when it was not raised in the High Court or in the petition for special leave.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the issue of misjoinder of charges is a substantive question and therefore, they should be at liberty to raise it at any stage, even for the first time before the Supreme Court.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, upheld by the court, was that the appellant cannot be permitted to raise this question at this stage as it was not urged in the High Court or taken in the petition for special leave.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a conviction for a substantive offence can be set aside due to the absence of, or an error in, the charge, without the accused demonstrating that prejudice was caused and a failure of justice occurred.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that the conviction was flawed because relevant questions showing the sharing of common intention were not put to the accused during questioning under Section 313 Cr.P.C., implying this procedural error was grounds to challenge the conviction.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, upheld by the court, was that such a contention does not merit acceptance. The implied argument is that an error or omission in the charge or related questioning is not fatal to the conviction unless the accused demonstrates that it caused prejudice and a failure of justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A procedural violation that is a mockery of a trial and abhorrent to the notions of natural justice will be struck down as illegal, as prejudice is patent. For other, less obvious violations, it must be determined whether prejudice was occasioned or if there was a reasonable probability of prejudice.
obiter: In borderline cases, very slight evidence of a reasonable possibility of prejudice would swing the balance in favour of the accused.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A conviction for a substantive offence will not be set aside due to an error, omission, or absence of a charge unless the accused can demonstrate that it has caused them actual prejudice and occasioned a failure of justice. The court distinguishes between fundamental violations that are inherently prejudicial, such as denying the accused a hearing, and other procedural errors where prejudice must be proven. Furthermore, the court will not normally consider grievances, such as misjoinder of charges, raised for the very first time at the Supreme Court stage.
legal_tests_applied: The Prejudice and Failure of Justice Test: Under Sections 215 and 464 of the Code, a conviction for a substantive offence without a charge can be set aside only if the accused shows that prejudice has been caused to him and that a “failure of justice” has occasioned thereby.

The Inherent Prejudice Test: Certain procedural violations are so vital or abhorrent to natural justice (e.g., refusal to give the accused a hearing, refusal to allow him to defend himself) that they are considered to have caused patent prejudice and are struck down at once, as they constitute a "mockery of a trial."
The Procedural Bar on New Arguments: Grievances not raised in the lower courts or in the petition for special leave are not normally considered for the first time by the Supreme Court.
why_appellant_lost: The plea of misjoinder of charges was not considered because it was raised for the first time before the Supreme Court, which is a practice the court does not normally permit.
The appellant failed to show that any prejudice was caused or that a failure of justice had been occasioned by the alleged error in the charge or the questioning under Section 313 Cr.P.C.

The court found that the gist of the charge sheet clearly alleged the sharing of common intention, meaning the appellant had knowledge of the exact nature of the charge against him, thus negating the claim of prejudice.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that the plea of misjoinder was raised too late was accepted, as the court follows the principle that such grievances are not normally considered when raised for the first time at the final appellate stage.

The respondent's position that an error in the charge is not fatal without proof of prejudice was upheld, as the court affirmed the legal principle that a conviction can only be set aside if the accused shows that a “failure of justice” has in fact been occasioned.
The court agreed with the respondent's implied position that no prejudice had occurred, finding that the appellant was made aware of the accusation of common intention through the charge sheet.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning distinguishes between procedural errors that are so fundamental they constitute a "mockery of a trial" and those where prejudice is not obvious. This ensures that only trials that are fundamentally unfair are struck down automatically, while other cases are decided on the actual impact of the error.

The requirement for an accused to demonstrate prejudice ensures that convictions are not overturned on mere technicalities, focusing the appellate review on whether a substantive failure of justice occurred.

The principle that the accused is entitled to know with certainty and accuracy the exact nature of the charge is upheld as a cornerstone of a fair trial, as without such knowledge, their defence will be prejudiced.
